THE RAILWAYS (OPENING FOR PUBLIC CARRIAGE OF PASSENGERS) 
RULES, 2000 
      The Railways (Opening for Public Carriage of Passengers) Rules, 2000 framed under 
the Railways Act. 1989 were examined and certain points were referred  to the Ministry 
of Railways for their comments/clarifications on the 2 nd May, 2001. The Ministry 
furnished their comments/clarifications on the 26th June, 2001. The points referred to the 
Ministry and their comments/clarifications thereon are reproduced below : 
I.    Point referred 

      The Rules have been framed under sections 28, 29, and 198 of the Railways Act, 1989. 
What are the reasons for framing the rules after a period of 11 years; In what manner 
Government have been regulating this area of activi ty so far. What are the reasons that 
necessitated the framing of these rules now? 
Minstry's reply 
      There existed "Rules for the Opening of a Railway or a Section of a Railway for the 
Public Carriage of Passengers of 1933" and they were in force till New Rules (2000) came 
into force. The new rules have been framed so as to bring them in line with new Railway 
Act of 1989. The exercise for framing of new rules took some time and hence the delay. 
II.  Point referred 
      Rule 2 (g) refers to the Indian Ra ilways (Open Lines) General Rule, 1976. Whether 
these rules have been validated under the Railways Act, 1989. If so, whether there was a 
similar Opening for Public carriage of passengers Rules under the old Act?. 
Ministry's reply 
      Yes, General Rules, 1976, have been validated under a notification in the official 
Gazette, as required under Section 60 & 87 of Indian Railway Act, 1989. 
      It is clarified that the General Rules are for guidance in the safe operation of Railways 
whereas "Rules for the Opening of a Railway or a section of a Railway for Public carriage 
of Passengers" are for guidance in checking and regulating fitness of a Railway line to 
run trains. 
General Rules existed before 1976 and were revised/updated in 1976. 
III.Point referred: Rule 15(2) List of questions and answers- 
"The Commissioner may, if he considers it necessary, modify the requirements 
specified in answers in accordance with the circumstances of each case." 
      Whether Government have any objection in prescribing that the Commissioner shall 
give in writing the reasons for modifying the requirements specified in the answers 
provided by the General Manager for consideration of the Commissioner in accordance 
with the circumstances of each case? 
Ministry's reply 
      Under Rule 15(1), the General Manager is required to submit answers to a list of 
questions regarding the Railway line. These questions concern the safety requirements. 
If Commissioner is not satisfied with the answers indicating the ground s ituation, the 
Commissioner can ask the General Manager to improve/modify the situation. No reasons 
are required to be stated by the Commissioner as the Commissioner checks the ground 
conditions only with respect to standards laid down by Railway Board. 
IV.Point referred: Rule 19 Documents accompanying Inspection Report- 
      "The following documents shall accompany the Inspection Report, namely:- 
(i)  Index Plan and Section of Railways; 
(ii)Tabulated details in Forms I to XIV; 
(iii)       List of Questions and Answers in Form XV; 
(iv)       Certificate by the General Manager of the concerned Railway in Form XVI; 
(v)List of infringements of Maximum and Minimum Dimensions in Form XVII; 
(vi)       Results of the Bridge Test in Form XVIII. 

Explanation- When sanction is required for the initiation of electric traction on a line 
already opened for passenger traffic, only such of the documents, as are required by 
the Commissioner, need be forwarded to him." 
      Whether the provision may be modified so as to speci fy the documents or type of 
documents required to be forwarded to the Commissioner for initiation of electric 
traction on a line to bring about uniformity in the rule? 
Ministry's reply 
      Explanation is slightly modified as under which explains the query:- 
Explanation-When sanction is required for the initiation of electric traction on a line 
already opened for passenger traffic, documents listed in Rule 5(1) at items (j), (k), 
(l), (m), (n) and rules 5(2) at (a) and 4(a)(vii) and as are required by the 
Commissioner, need be forwarded to him. 
V.  Point referred: Rule 20 Sanction of Report to Central Government- 
"In respect of every reference made to him under sub -fule (3) of rule 3, the 
Commissioner shall submit an Inspection Report to the Central Government." 
      Whether under this rule it is possible to prescribe a maximum time limit which the 
Commissioner may be required to submit the Inspection Report so that there is timely 
opening of the railway line? Should provision be made for extension of time only after 
giving reasons for the same? Whether also the Inspection Report may be considered to 
be a public document and whether a copy thereof should be given to   the General 
Manager of the Zonal Railway/Chief Engineer of non-Government Railway? 
      Whether Government should not give opportunity to Chief Engineer of non 
Government Railway before modifying or cancelling a sanction? 
Ministry's reply 
      It is not proposed to specify a time limit as Commissioner will submit his report within 
a reasonable time. Besides CCRS oversees the work of Commissioner. As far as opening 
of railway is concerned, the powers are proposed to be conferred on Commissioner to 
open the railway under Section 28 of IR Act, 1989 by modifying rule 22. 
      While the Report of Commissioner on inspection of a railway is not a public document 
and is not recommended to be made so, a copy is always given to General Manager of 
Zonal Railway/Non-government Railway. 
      The matter concerns safety. Only in extreme situation, act ion of cancellation of 
sanction will be taken by Commissioner/Government. 
VI.Point referred: Rule 21(3) Sanctioning of Opening of Railway- 
      In respect of non Government railway in fule 21(3) the words "General Manager" 
appear to be an error. 
Ministry's reply 
      There is no error. The definition of 'General Manager' as per rule 2(f) covers the Chief 
Executive of Non-government Railway. 
VII.   Point referred: Rule 22(2) Temporary opening of railways by Commissioner- 
      "On receipt of the Inspection Report of Commissioner, the Central Government may 
confirm, modify or cancel the sanction given under sub - rule (1) subject to such 
conditions, alterations or relaxation as may be considered necessary." 

      Whether the provision may be modified so that the Central Government shall record 
reasons for modifying or cancelling the sanction given under sub-rule (1)? 
Ministry's reply 
      This being a matter of safety, decision of Government is final and binding. No 
reasoning need be given for Government decision. 
VIII.Point referred : Rule 24(4) Notice of construction of deviation lines, etc.- 
"In case of an accident, temporary diversions may be opened under section 24 after 
a responsible officer of the concerned railway certifies that the use of such diversion 
will not be attended with danger to passengers or to the railway servants." 
      The use of the term "responsible" in the rule is vague. Should the designation/rank of 
the responsible officer as provided for in the rule may not be specified? 
Ministry's reply 
      Section 24 of Indian Railways Act, 1989 states that this certificate has to be given by 
Railway servant in charge of works undertaken. The rule is framed under Section 24 of 
IR Act, 1989 and therefore the connotation of "responsible officer" h ere is "Railway 
servant in charge of works". 
IX.Point referred : Rule 24(5) Notice of construction of deviation lines, etc.- 
    "Where the use of the temporary diversion is likely to be extended to for more 
than three days, the Commissioner shall take act ion to inspect the diversion at the 
earliest opportunity." 
      The term "earliest opportunity" as used in the rule is vague. Whether the term may 
be substituted with words which may specify that action is taken within a time frame 
between period of intimation of diversion and use of such temporary diversion to ensure 
prompt action on the part of the Commissioner? 
Ministry's reply 
      It is proposed to modify this rule. The modified version will follow. 
X.  Point referred: Rule 25(1) Power of Commissioner to open minor works- 
    "The Commissioner may, without previous notice, sanction the opening of any 
minor work for passenger traffic, if he is satisfied. either with or without inspection, 
that the provisions of clauses (b), (c) and (d) of sub section (1) of section 22 have been 
duly fulfilled." 
      What is the definition of "minor work" needs to be defined or referred to? 
Ministry's reply 
      The minor works are defined in Rule 24. 
XI.Point referred: Rule 31(5) Signals 
"It is desirable that the signaling at all block stations and interlocked level crossings 
in the same section shall conform to the same standard and type." 
      Whether Government have any objection in deleting the words "It is desirable that" 
to make it comp ulsory for signaling at all block stations in the same section and inter 
locked level crossings to conform to the same standard and type.? 
Ministry's reply 

      Signaling improvements cannot be implemented in one go. Therefore, such a 
compulsory provision cannot be made. 
XII.   Point referred: Rule 38(2) (a) Designs of electric installations- 
    "Adequate protective arrangements shall be made to ensure that the public cannot 
come in contact with the electric equipment on line within the railway premises." 
      The term "adequate protective arrangements" is vague. Whether Government have 
any objection if arrangements or at least their nature required to be fulfilled for public 
safety are enlisted/stated in the rule itself? 
Ministry's reply 
      Need to changes is not felt as it is difficult to define the precautions to be taken in each 
and every situation nor it is the purpose of the rules. 
2.   The Committee considered the comments of the Ministry on the questionnaire at its 
meetings held on the 7th May 2003. The Committee notes with satisfaction that the 
Ministry of Railways have accepted the Committee's suggestions on (i) Rule 19 
Explanation to modify the provision so as to specify the documents or types of 
documents required to be forwarded to the Commissioner for initiation of electric 
traction on a line; and (ii) Rule 24(5) to substitute the words earliest opportunity with 
suitable words so as to specify that the action is taken within a time frame between 
period of initiation of diversion and use of such temporary diversion to ensure prompt 
action on the part of the Commissioner. The Committee however, recommends that 
Rule 24(4) may be amended by substituting the words "responsible officer" with the 
words "Railway servant in charge of the work" in view of their comments. The 
Committee hopes that the Ministry would carry out these amendments expeditiously 
under intimation to it.

THE COMPANIES (ISSUE OF SHARE CAPITAL WITH DIFFERENTIAL VOTING 
RIGHTS) RULES, 2001 
      The Committee examined the Companies (Issue of Share Capital with Differential 
Voting Rights) Rules, 2001 framed under the Companies Act, 1956. Certain points were 
referred to the Department of Company Affairs for their comments on the 5th October, 
2001. The points raised and the Department's commen ts thereon received on the 29th 
October, 2001 are reproduced below. 
I.  Point referred Rule 2(I)(b) 
    "Differential voting rights includes rights as to dividend or voting". The meaning 
of words, 'Differential Voting Rights' is not clear. A detailed note explaining the same 
may be furnished. 
Department's reply 
      Shares with Differential Voting Rights means shares which carry different rights from 
that of one -share one-vote. It may be even non -voting shares i.e. persons having such 
shares shall have no right to vote at the time of poll in a meeting of the share holders. The 
financing needs of the companies have become too complex to be met only with two types 
of shares i.e. equity shares and preference shares . In many countries, corporate growth 
has been accompanied by introduction of various forms of securities including issue of 
shares with differential rights. On demand of trade and industry and in view of that some 

of shareholders are not interested in exe rcising their voting rights like other equity 
shareholders, it was provided in the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2000 to allow 
companies to issue shares (i) with voting rights or (ii) with differential rights as to 
dividend voting or otherwise. Before this amendment companies were not allowed to issue 
equity shares without or with voting rights less than one vote per share. It is expected that 
introduction of shares with differential voting rights will permit the growth and 
expansion of companies. The shares w ith differential voting rights would bring in more 
share capital for companies for their projects and activities from those sections of 
investors also are basically interested in higher rate of dividend and are prepared for a 
trade off between dividend and voting power since shares with differential voting rights 
could carry higher dividend than that of equity shares with full voting rights. This concept 
is not entirely new since Indian companies are already allowed to raise capital through 
preference shares and debt instruments which have no voting rights. Such shareholders, 
excepting for their difference in voting rights, will enjoy all other rights like any other 
shareholder including right for bonus shares. right shares and to have annual returns, 
etc. of the company. Such shares will be quoted in Stock Exchanges and, therefore, there 
will be a right market for them specially when they are offered higher dividend. 
II.  Points referred Rule 3(1) & (2) 
    "The Company has distributable profits in terms of Section 205 of the Companies 
Act, 1956 for Preceding three financial years preceding the year in which it was 
decided to issue such shares". The word 'preceding' before the words 'three financial 
years' appears to be superfluous, Whether the Ministry have any objection in 
deleting it? 
"The company has not defaulted in filing annual accounts and annual returns for 
three financial years immediately preceding the financial years of the year in which 
it was decided to issue such shares". The words 'of the year' after the words 'financial 
year' appear to be superfluous; whether the Ministry have any objection in deleting 
these words? 
Department's reply 
      Department accepts the suggestion to delete the word "preceding" before the words 
"three financial years" in Rule 3(1) and the words "of the year" after the words 
"financial year" in Rule 3(2) of the said Rules. Action is being taken to amend the said 
Rules. A copy of Notification of amended Rules shall be furnished to the Rajya Sabha 
Secretariat after the Notification is issued to amend the said Rules. 
2.   The Department of Company Affairs furnished a copy of the Notification G.S.R. 27 
(E) dated 12th January, 2002 notifying the amendments as suggested by the Committee. 
3.   The Committee considered the matter at its meeting held on the 25th October 2002. 
The Committee is satisfied to note that the Department of Company Affairs have 
notified the amendments as suggested by the Committee by deleting the word 
"preceding" in rule 3(1) and the words "of the year" in rule 3(2) which were 
superfluous.

      I, the Chairman of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, having been authorized 
by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Hundred 
and Fiftieth Report of the Committee. 
.

December, 2003.

2.   During the course of scrutiny of these Orders, the Committee ha s noted some cases 
where there has been a considerable time lag between the date of notification of the Order 
and the date of its laying. The annexed statement also indicates the period of delay in 
cases where notifications have not been laid as per the Co mmittee’s guidelines and 
whether such notifications were accompanied by a statement indicating the reasons for 
the delay in laying. In some of the cases the delay has been quite abnormal. The 
observations/recommendations of the Committee in respect of the specific 
Ministries/Departments are as follows:-    
  
(i)  Ministry of Agriculture 

    (Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying) 
  
         The Committee notes that the laying of   notification at Sl. No.7 of the  
Annexure by   the Ministry of Agricultur e (Department of Animal Husbandry and 
Dairying)  has been delayed   by 6 months.   Having been  notified on the 19 th February, 
2003 the regulation could have been laid during the Budget Session itself. The Ministry 
have even failed to append the delay statement to the notification.  The Committee hopes 
that the Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying) would 
adhere to the time schedule as recommended by it in the matter of laying of 
the  Subordinate Legislation pertaining to their Department.  
  
(ii)     Ministry of Civil Aviation 
  
      The Committee regrets to note that the Ministry of Civil Aviation have delayed the 
laying of one of their notifications (Sl. no. 9) out of the 10 notifications laid by them during 
the 199 th  session.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry   of Civil Aviation 
should stick to the time schedule as recommended by the it in its 131 st  Report in laying 
the Subordinate Legislation before the Parliament. 
  
(iii)       Ministry of Communications and Information  Technology 
  
            The Committee regrets to find that out of the 5 notifications laid by the Ministry 
of Communications and Information Technology, there has been  a delay in two cases (Sl. 
Nos.32 & 33 of the Annexure) and no delay statement has been appended therewith.  Two 
notifications (Sl. 35 & 36) laid by the Ministry of Communication and Information 
Technology bear identical notification Nos.. Such notifications in future should bear the 
distinct  Nos.35 and 36 for easier identi fication. The Committee expects the Ministry of 
Communications and Information Technology, etc. to exercise caution in such   matters 
for future and ensure that the schedule as prescribed by it in the matter of laying of 
subordinate legislation framed under various Acts of Parliament is followed meticulously. 
  
(iv)       Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution 
  
            The Committee is unhappy to note that the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food 
& Public Distribution have delayed the laying of 3 of their notifications  (Sl.No. 37, 41 & 
42) out of the 8 notifications laid by them during the Session. The Ministry have not 
appended delay statement with two notifications which are  at Sl. no.   37 and 41. The 
Committee would like to draw attention of  the Ministry towards the schedule  prescribed 
by it in the matter of laying of Subordinate Legislation and it hopes that this would be 
complied with in future. 
  
(v)        Ministry of Environment & Forests 
  
      The Committee notes that the Ministry of Environment and Forests have delayed 
laying of 1 of their notifications (Sl. no 49) out of the 7 notifications (Sl. nos. 46 to 52) laid 
by them during the session and no delay statements had been appended therewith. The 
Committee hopes that the Ministry of Environment and Forests would observe the time 
schedule prescribed by it for laying of Subordinate Legislation in future.  
  
  
  
  

  
(vi)                   Ministry of Finance 
                         
            The Committee is unhappy to no te that the Ministry of Finance have delayed 
laying of 33of their notifications (Sl. No. 56, 63, 65, 78-99, 103, 170,171 and 233-236),  out 
of 236 notifications laid by them during the 199 th Session.  The above notifications has 
been delayed by the period ranging from 4 month to 2 years and 7 months.  The Ministry 
of Finance have not appended delay statement  in some of the cases.  In this connection it 
may be mentioned here that there was   delay in laying in case of 77 and 47 notification 
laid during the 197th & 198th Session respectively.  Attention of the Ministry is also invited 
to the G.S.R. 115 (E)   dated the 21 st February, 2003 and G.S.R. 217 (E) dated the 17 th 
March, 2003 (Sl. No. 170 and 171 respectively).  Both the notifications bear identical short 
title.  It would be more appropriate if such notifications are distinguished by numbering 
as ‘first amendment’ and ‘second amendment’ and so on. The Committee obse rved that 
the Ministry of Finance do not strictly adhere to the time schedule prescribed in its 135th 
Report.   The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Finance would make special efforts 
to avoid  such instances of delay in future. 
  
(vii)      Ministry of Home Affairs 
  
            The Committee regrets to note that the Ministry of Home Affairs have 
delayed  laying of two notifications (Sl. No. 305 and306) out of   twelve notifications laid 
during the Session. The Ministry have failed to enclose the delay statement  except one 
notifications at Sl. No. 306 of the Annexure.    The Committee hopes that the Ministry of 
Home Affairs shall in future comply with the schedule prescribed by the Committee in 
this behalf in its 131st Report presented to House on 15th December, 2000. 
  
  
(viii)      Ministry of Human Resource & Development 
            (Department of Elementary Education and Literacy) 
  
            The Committee regret to note that the Ministry of Human Resource Development 
(Department of Elementary Education and Literacy) have again delayed laying of   two 
out of three notifications (Sl.nos. 307 & 308) laid during the Session by more than 5 
months and no delay statement is appended therewith. The Committee impressed upon 
the Ministry of Human Resource Development (Department of Elementary Education 
and Literacy) to pay adequate attention towards   the timely laying   of the subordinate 
legislations. 
  
  
 (ix)      Ministry of Labour 
  
            The Committee notes with regret the delay of 4 months in laying of one notification 
(Sl. no. 313) out of 3 notifications laid by the Ministry.   The Ministry have also not 
appended the delay statement.   The Committee    hopes that the Ministry would take 
precaution to avoid recurrence of such instances. 
  
(x)        Ministry of Law & Justice 
  
The Committee notes with regret that out of two notifications laid during the 
Session, there is delay of almost 6 years in case of one notification which is not justified. 

(Sl. no. 314). The Committee hopes that the Ministry  shall adhere to the time schedule as 
recommended by it for laying  the Subordinate Legislation before the Parliament.  
  
(xi)       Ministry of  Personnel, Public Grievances & Pension 
  
            The Committee notes with regret that the Ministry of Personnel, Public 
Grievances & Pension have laid 6 notifications during the  session out of which 3  (Sl. Nos. 
316 to 318) have been delayed by a period  of 4 months.  Further,  the Ministry have not 
appended delay statement, there wer e instances of delay during the 191 st to 193 rd and 
197th Session also. The Committee expects the Ministry to be cautious in such matters and 
ensure compliance of time schedule for laying of the notifications in future.  
  
  
(xii)      Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas 
  
            The Committee regrets to note that the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas have 
laid two notifications during the 199th Session and  one of them has been delayed by more 
than 7 months (Sl. No. 322). The Committee directs the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural 
Gas to avoid recurrence of such instances in future. 
  
(xiii)      Ministry of Power 
  
The Committee notes with regret that there is delay in laying   of one  out of the 4 
notifications laid by the Ministry of Power by 4   months (Sl. No. 324) and the Ministry 
have not appended any delay statement. The Committee also finds that Sl. nos. 324 & 326 
and Sl. nos. 325 and 327 are showing similar notification numbers.   The notification 
should bear distinct numbers for easier identifica tion.  The Committee hopes that the 
Ministry would   ensure strict compliance of the schedule for laying Subordinate 
Legislation as prescribed by the Committee  in its 131st report.  
  
  
(xiv)     Ministry of Road Transport & Highways 
  
            The Committee notes that the Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways  have  again delayed in laying of 18 notifications (Sl. Nos. 328 -340, 365-367 & 
393 and 394) out of the total of 77 notifications laid. The delay in laying   ranges from 3 
months to one year 4 months and they have not   appended delay statements in case of 5 
notifications (Sl. nos. 365-367,393 & 394). The Committee expects the Ministry to be more 
prompt and vigilant in laying the rules/regulations within the stipulated period to obviate 
such instances of delay in future. 
  
            Besides the above,   the Committee also notes with regret   the isolated cases of 
delayed laying of notifications by the Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty 
Alleviation (Sl. No. 410 of the Annexure).   The Committee would like the Ministries to 
take note of the time schedule which is reproduced hereinafter and ensure that the same 
is complied with meticulously in    future.  The Committee, accordingly,   reiterates its 
observations made in its 135th Report. 
  
  
“The Committee has, time and again, emphasized that it is essential that in case there is 
a delay in the laying of Statutory Orders, the concerned Ministry/Department should 
invariably append a delay statement along with the notifications being laid so as to 

apprise Parliament of the causes of delay. The Committee desires all 
Ministries/Departments to take a note of this, since the intention is that through the 
process of formulation of a delay statement the Ministry is able to introspect, identifying 
bottlenecks and devise remedial measures”.  
  
.           The Committee impresses upon all the Ministries/Departments to take immediate 
steps to avoid delay in laying of Subordinate Legislation. The Committee, accordingly, 
wishes to bring to the notice of all Minis tries/Departments of the Government of India, 
particularly, the defaulting ones as enumerated above the following recommendations, as 
contained in its 131 st Report wherein a time schedule for the laying of Subordinate 
legislation has been prescribed,  as follows: 
  
“Orders required to be laid before the House should be laid (i) if the House is not in 
Session, during the Session immediately following the date of publication of the Order in 
the Official Gazette and (ii) if the House is in Session, on the date of the publication of the 
Order, during its continuance and in case the time lag between the date of publication 
and the date of the closing of the Session is less than 15 clear days, before the expiry of 
the Session immediately following the said Session . All the Ministries/Departments of 
Government of India should henceforth comply with this schedule in the matter of laying 
of the orders issued under various Acts of Parliament on the Table of the Rajya Sabha.”

I 
Mineral Concession Rules, 1960

October, 2001.  The Committee discussed the matter with the representatives of the 
National Mineral Development Corporation and the Ministry of Mines and the Ministry 
of Steel at Hyderabad on the 8th November 2001. The points referred to theMinistry, 
their comments/ clarifications and the observations of the Committee thereon are 
reproduced below: 
  
I           Point referred  
            Whether the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 and amendment thereto have been 
laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha and    if so, the date of laying thereof?   
  
            Ministry’s reply 
            The Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 (MCR, 1960) were laid on the Table of the 
Rajya Sabha on the 6th December 1960, and all amendments thereto have been 
regularly laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha, the last amendment in Mineral 
Concession Rules, 1960 dated the 22nd January 2001 was laid in Rajya Sabha on the 2nd 
March 2001. 
  
Committee’s observations 
            The Committee noted that the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 and amendments 
thereto were laid on time.  
  
II         Point referred Rule 9 (2) (a): - Application fee 
             
            “A fee calculated in accordance with the provisions of Schedule II.” 
  
               The amount of application fee indicated in Schedule II are nominal. Whether 
Government have any objection in increasing the amount of application to @Rs.500/- 
for first square Km. and Rs.100/- for each additional square Km or any other 
reasonable amounts? 
  
Ministry’s reply 

The Department of Mines may have no objection to an increase in fees payable. 
The Department of Mines has received representations from various State 
Governments also that the application fees are meager and these should be suitably 
enhanced. The matter is already under examination in the Department. However, while 
fixing these rates, it may be kept in view that the fees, by their very nature, are designed 
to cover mainly the processing costs, and, therefore, increasing the existing rates, i.e, to 
Rs 250 for first square kilometer or part thereof, and Rs 50 for each additional square 
kilometer seem justified. 
            Committee’s observations 
            The Committee noted with satisfaction that the Ministry had accepted the 
Committee's suggestion regarding suitable revision of application fee.  
  
III        Point referred Rule 9 (2) (d) and Rule 22 (3) (d): -  Valid clearance certificate 
  
               Rule 9(2)(d)  
               "Every application shall be accompanied by a valid clearance certificate, in the 
form prescribed by the State Government, of payment of mining dues, such as royalty 
or dead rent and surface rent payable under the Act or the rules made thereunder, from 
the Government or any officer of authority by that Government in this behalf.” 
Rule 22(3)(d)  
"Every application for the grant or renewal of a mining lease shall be 
accompanied by a valid clearance certificate, in the form prescribed by the State 
Government of payment of mining dues, such as royalty or dead rent and surface rent 
payable under the Act or the rules made thereunder, from the Government or any 
officer or authority authorized by that Government in this behalf.” 
What is the justification for authorizing the State Governments to prescribe the 
form of clearance certificate; whether Government has any objection in prescribing the 
form in the rules itself? 
Ministry’s reply 
The form of the valid clearance certificate depends on the manner of collection of 
the amounts payable under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 
1957 and the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960. Rule 64 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 
1960 empowers the State Governments to specify the manner of collection of the mining 
dues. The State Governments also notify the Minor Mineral Concession Rules in 
exercise of powers under section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and 

Regulation) Act, 1957, and generally specify similar modes of collection of mining dues 
for major minerals under rule 64 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 and for minor 
minerals under the State Minor Mineral Concession Rules. Since the manner of 
collecting fees and deposits vary from State to State, as per the convenience of the State 
concerned, the format of the clearance certificate has not been specified in the Mineral 
Concession Rules, 1960. It is felt, specifying the format may impinge upon the 
delegation of powers already enjoyed by the States. 
            Committee’s observations 
            The Committee noted the Ministry's reply. 
  
IV        Point referred Rule 9 (3): - 
  
“The State Government may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, relax the 
provisions of clause (d) of sub-rule (2) of Rule 9.” 
What are the circumstances under which the State Government may relax the 
provisions of Rule 9 (2) (d) and whether Government have any objection in indicating 
the nature/type of such circumstances in the rules itself? 
Ministry’s reply 
Rule 9(2) (d) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 states that the application 
for prospecting license should be accompanied by a valid clearance certificate of the 
payment of mining dues. Rule 9(3) empowers the State Governments to relax this 
condition for reasons to be recorded in writing.  
            The instances in which the State Governments use the discretionary power to 
relax the condition are recorded in the case files maintained by the States, and the 
instances of such relaxation come to the notice of the Central Government only if any of 
such cases are challenged in Revision Applications. The State Governments have been 
seen to use the discretionary power in cases where the applicant had paid dues and 
could produce counterfoils of treasury challans to that effect, although the competent 
authority had not formally issued the clearance certificate, cases where the certificate 
could not be furnished by all members of the partnership firm or all members of the 
private limited company in time, or in cases where the party fails, despite best efforts, to 
produce the valid clearance certificate within ninety days of giving a sworn affidavit 
that no dues are outstanding, for reasons like illness. 
  
            Since use of the discretionary power to relax requirement of a valid clearance 
certificate along with an application for grant of renewal of a prospecting license is 

entirely in the revenue interest of the State Government, it is perhaps not necessary to 
lay down strict conditions for allowing such relaxation. The provision that the reasons 
for relaxation should be recorded in writing is enough safeguards that the power is not 
misused, and also provides flexibility to the State Government to attend to genuine 
difficulties. 
  
Committee’s observations 
The Committee noted the Ministry's reply.  
  
V         Point referred Rule 14 (1) (i): -         Conditions of a prospecting   licence 
  
           “The licensee shall pay such prospecting fee as may be fixed by the State 
Government, being not less than fifty paise and not more than five rupees per hectare 
of land covered by the license for each year or part of a year of the period for which 
the license is granted or renewed.”  
  
           The rule provides very nominal amount of prospecting fee to be paid by the 
licensee.  Whether Government have any objection in raising the prospecting fee up to 
a reasonable level which is relevant to the current times? 
  
Ministry’s reply 
The prospecting fee has been deliberately kept at a nominal amount since the 
licensee does not win any mineral on the basis of prospecting, and there are no 
commercial gains from prospecting exercises. Moreover, if the licensee wins minerals in 
excess of what is provided in the rules, he is liable to pay royalty. Therefore, in 
consideration of the fact that these rates were fixed decades ago, the fee payable may be 
increased to not less than Rupee one and not more than rupees ten per hectare of land.   
  
            Committee’s observations 
            The Committee was satisfied to note that the Ministry has agreed to revise the 
prospecting fees as suggested by it.  
  
VI        Point referred Rule 20 (1): -              Security deposit 
  
           “An application for a prospecting license shall, before the deed referred to in 
sub-rule (1) of rule 15 is executed, deposit a security for the due observance of the 

terms and conditions of the license a sum of five hundred rupees in respect of every 
square kilometer or part thereof for which the license is granted.” 
  
           The rule, provides very meagre amount of security deposit for due observance of 
the terms and conditions of the licence. Whether Government has any objection in 
raising this amount suitably?    
  
Ministry’s reply 
The Department of Mines has no objection, and a security deposit up to Rupees 
2500 appears reasonable. 
             
Committee’s observations 
            The Committee was satisfied to note that the Ministry had no objection in raising 
the amount of security deposit as suggested by it.  
  
VII         Point referred     Rule 22 (1) and (3) (i) (a): -         Application fee 
for   grant    of    mining lease  
  
           “Rule 22(1): An     application for the grant of a mining lease in respect of land 
in which the minerals vested in the Government shall be made to the State Government 
in Form I through such officer or authority as the State Government may specify in 
this behalf.” 
  
           “Rule 22(3)(i)(a) : Every application for the grant of renewal of a mining lease 
shall be accompanied by – a fee of five hundred rupees” 
  
(i)                  Rule 22 (1) does not prescribe any application fee for grant of mining lease. 
(ii)                The amount of fee for renewal of a mining lease is meagre.  
  
Whether Government have any objection in prescribing the amount of 
application fee for grant of a mining lease as well as raising the amount of fee for 
renewal of a mining lease? 
  
Ministry’s reply 
Rule 22(1) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 prescribes the procedure of 
application for grant of mining lease while rule 22(3) prescribes the documents and 
other accompaniments to such an application for mining lease. The application fee for 

grant of mining lease is already prescribed in rule 22(3) (i) and there is perhaps no 
separate advantage in doing so in rule 22(1) itself. 
  
The Department of Mines has received representations from various State 
Governments also that the application fees are meager and these should be suitably 
enhanced. The matter is already under examination in the Department.  
  
            Committee’s observations 
            The Committee noted with satisfaction that the Ministry has agreed to revise the 
application fees for grant of mining lease as suggested by it.   
  
VIII   Point referred Dead Rent: - 
  
The term `Dead Rent’ has been used at a number of places in the rules like rules 
9 (2) (d), 22 (3) (d), (27), etc.  The meaning of these words is not clear.  Whether 
Government has any objection in defining the terms `Dead Rent’, in the rules itself? 
  
Ministry’s reply 
The term "dead rent" is defined in Law in precise terms, and therefore the term 
was not separately defined in the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) 
Act, 1957 or in the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960. For instance, Osborn's Concise 
Law Dictionary (Universal Law Publishing Co. Pvt Ltd, 1993) defines "dead rent" as 
the minimum rent payable under a mining lease, irrespective of whether minerals are 
won or not'. Also, so far, no instances have come to the notice of the Central 
Government where the definition and application of the term dead rent as used in the 
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 and the Mineral 
Concession Rules, 1960, have been challenged in any court of law. 
  
            Committee’s observations 
            The Committee was not satisfied with the Ministry's comments and desired that 
they may examine the possibility of defining the term in the Rules itself.  
  
IX        Point referred Rule 22 (3): -  (last proviso) 
             
            “Provided that the applicant shall   deposit such further deposit as may be asked 
for by the State Government, within one month from the date of demand of such 
deposit.” 

  
            The proviso does not mention any purpose for which the applicant is required to 
make further deposit.  Whether Government have any objection in mentioning the 
purpose for such further deposit is required? 
  
Ministry’s reply 
Rule 22 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 relates to application for grant of 
mining leases. Rule 22(3)(i) prescribes that an application fee and inter alia a valid 
clearance certificate shall accompany the application. Rule 22(3) (ii) provides that apart 
from these, a deposit shall accompany for meeting the preliminary expenses in 
connection with the grant of mining lease. The proviso to this Rule prescribes that the 
applicant shall deposit such further deposit as may be asked for by the State 
Government, and it is, therefore, clear that the purpose for such additional demand is 
only for meeting additional expenses in connection with the grant of mining lease. The 
expenses in connection with the grant of mining lease depend on the size of the area, and 
the topography. The State Government is required to deploy staff for surveying and 
measuring angles for demarcation of the area and expenses connected with such 
demarcation vary from area to area and hence it may be necessary to ask for a deposit 
over and above Rs 1000 as provided for in the rules in specific cases.  
             
Committee’s observations 
The Committee noted the Ministry's reply. 
  
X         Point referred Rule 27 (1) (f) and 28 (1): - 
  
            Rule 27 (1) (f) 
"the lessee shall commence mining operations within one year from the date of 
execution of the lease and shall thereafter conduct such operations in a proper, skillful 
and workman-like manner.” 
  
            Rule 28 (1) 
"Subject to the other conditions of this rule where mining operations are not 
commenced within a period of two years from the date of execution of the lease, or is 
discontinued for a continuous period of two years after commencement of such 
operations, the State Government shall, by an order, declare the mining lease as lapsed 
and communicate the declaration to the lessee.” 

  
(i)                  Whether there are any guidelines and norms for conducting mining operations 
in a proper, skillful and workman-like manner as provided in rule 27(1)(f)? 
  
(ii)                Provisions of rule 27 (1) (f) and 28 (1) are contradictory:  On one hand, it is 
mandatory on the part of a lessee to commence mining operation within one year from 
the date of execution of the lease while on the other hand a mining lease shall be 
declared as lapsed if mining operations are not commenced within a period of two years 
from the date of execution of the lease.  Whether Government has any objection in 
rectifying the position? 
  
Ministry’s reply 
There appears to be a typographical error in rule 27 (1) (f) as has been presented 
for comments, since the rule already provides that the lessee shall commence mining 
operations within two years from the date of execution of the mining lease. 
             
            The guidelines and norms for conducting mining operations in proper skilful and 
workmanlike manner are provided in the Mineral Conservation and Development 
Rules, 1988, framed under section 18 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and 
Regulation) Act, 1957, and these rules have been already reviewed by the Committee on 
Subordinate Legislation of the Rajya Sabha. 
  
            Committee’s observations 
            The Committee noted the Ministry's reply.  
  
XI        Point referred Terms `Determination’ and `Determine’: - 
  
At a number of places terms `Determination’ and `Determine’ have been used in 
the rules like rules 27, 29, etc. Meanings of those terms are not clear. Whether 
Government has any objection in defining these terms in the rules itself? 
  
Ministry’s reply 
The term "determination" is defined in Law in precise terms, and, therefore, the 
term was not separately defined in the Mines and Minerals (Development and 
Regulation) Act, 1957 or in the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960. For instance Osborn's 
Concise Law Dictionary (Universal Law Publishing Co. Pvt Ltd, 1993) defines 
"determination" as "to come to an  end". Also, so far no instances have come to the 

notice of the Central Government where the definition and application of the term 
determination or determine as used in the Mines and Minerals (Development and 
Regulation) Act, 1957 and the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 have been challenged.  
  
            Committee’s observations 
            The Committee was not satisfied with the Ministry's Comments and directed 
that they may re-examine the feasibility of defining these terms in the Rules.  
  
XII      Point referred  
  
Section 4A of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 
provides for termination of prospecting licenses or mining leases.  But the Mineral 
Concession Rules, 1960 not provide anywhere in this regard. Whether Government 
would clarify the position? 
  
Ministry’s reply 
The Section 4A of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 
1957 provides the general restrictions of the circumstances in which, in the interest of 
regulation of mines and mineral development etc, preservation of natural environment, 
public health etc, the prospecting licenses or the mining leases may be terminated. The 
Provisions already made in the Act have not been replicated in the rules, the former 
being the principal legislation.   
  
            Committee’s observations 
            The Committee noted the Ministry's reply. 
  
  
XIII     Point referred Rule 29 (1) (a): - Restriction on determination of lease 
  
            “Rule 29(1)(a) The lessee applies for such surrender of mineral at least 6 months 
before the intended date of surrender.” 
  
(b)                                *            *               * 
  
Provided also that surrender of the lease area by the lessee shall be permitted 
only thrice during the period of the lease on fulfilling the conditions -  that at least a 
period of five years has  elapsed since the last surrender.” 
             

What is the objective sought to be achieved by the above provisions.  The period 
of 6 months for applying surrender of mineral before the intended date of surrender 
and the period of five years for allowing next surrender of a mineral are unreasonably 
on the higher side.  Whether Government has any objection in reducing these periods to 
two months and two years, respectively? 
  
Ministry’s reply 
If a mining lease is granted for a group of minerals, the notice period of six 
months has no adverse repercussion on the lessee, because no royalty will be charged if 
the particular mineral is not produced. However, the surrender of mineral requires a 
notice of six months at least in order to enable the State Government to process the 
application, and satisfy itself that the mineral has been actually depleted for economic 
exploitation, for any such surrender depicts revenue loss to the State Government. 
Already in case of the area being properly surveyed and being contiguous, such 
surrender is permitted from the date of the receipt of the application. Further, the 
lesseealso has to fulfil the condition ofrule 23 of the Mineral Conservation and 
Development Rules, 1988, under which in the interest of mineral conservation, for 
which a duty has been cast upon the Central Government by the Parliament, Central 
Government, through the Indian Bureau of Mines is also required to satisfy itself to 
prohibit such abandonment or allow abandonment with such conditions as may be 
specified in the permission. MCDR requires a notice of ninety days before abandonment 
of mining for the Central Government to complete the process of evaluation.  
  
Further, under rule 34 of Mineral Conservation and Development Rules, 1988, 
the lessee is required to undertake the phased reclamation and rehabilitation of land 
affected by mining operations, which is required to be completed before the conclusion 
of such operations and abandonment of mines.  
  
In order to enable all competent authorities to complete various duties assigned 
to them the notice period of six months is considered adequate. 
  
Surrender of area being permissible one in five years is linked to the provision of 
Scheme of mining, which is submitted every five years. Logically, at the time of 
submitting the scheme of mining for next five years, depletion of any mineral would also 

be planned for. These provisions act as checks and measures against possible slaughter 
mining and help in mineral conservation.    
  
            Committee’s observations 
            The Committee noted the Ministry's reply. 
  
XIV     Point referred Rule 37 (2) and Rule 45(ii):- 
  
Rule 37 (2) 
"Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-rule (1) the lessee may, subject to the 
conditions specified in the proviso to rule 35, transfer his lease or any right, title or 
interest therein to a person   who has filed an affidavit stating that he has filed an up-
to-date income tax return, paid the income tax assessed on him and paid the income tax

Rule 45 (ii)

            The above rules refer proviso to Rule 35, but Rule 35 has already been

Ministry’s reply 
It is correct to state that the erstwhile rule 35 of Mineral Concession Rules, 1960

from rule 37 (2) vide GSR 743 (E) dated the 25th September 2000, but inadvertently the 
reference continues in rule 45 (ii). The inadvertent mistake is being rectified.  
  
            Committee’s observations 
            The Committee noted with satisfaction that the Ministry has agreed to rectify 
reference to an omitted rule, which was inadvertent.

            “The licensee shall pay the granter such prospecting fee as may be agreed upon, 
being not less than fifty paise and not more than five rupees per hectare of the land 

covered by the license for each year or a part of the year of the period for which a 
license is granted or renewed.” 
  
            The amount of prospecting fee prescribed in the above rule is meagre.  Whether 
Government has any objection in raising the amount suitably? 
  
Ministry’s reply 
The prospecting fee has been deliberately kept at a nominal amount since the 
licensee does not win any mineral on the basis of prospecting, and there are no 
commercial gains from prospecting exercises. Moreover, if the licensee wins minerals in 
excess of what is provided in the rules, he is liable to pay royalty. Therefore, in 
consideration of the fact that these rates were fixed decades ago, the fee payable may be

XVI     Point referred Proviso under Rule 59 (1) (e) (ii): - 
  
“Provided further that where an area reserved under rule 58, (or under section 
17A of the Act) is proposed to be granted to a Government Company, no notification 
under clause (ii) shall be required to be issued. 
  
The above proviso refers to Rule 58, which has already been omitted. Whether 
Government has any objection in modifying the provisions suitably? 
  
Ministry’s reply 
Section 17A of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, 
as amended since 25th January, 1994 lays down the provisions under which mineral 
bearing areas can be reserved by the Government. While such areas can be reserved by 
the Central Government, in consultation with the State Government, under sub-section 
17A (1) for conservation purposes, under subsection 17A (1A), the Central Government 
can reserve mineral bearing areas for exploitation by the Central Public Sector 
Undertakings. Under subsection 17A (2), the State Governments can reserve areas for 

exploitation by the State Public Sector Undertakings, after obtaining approval of the 
Central Government for the same.  
  
However, prior to 22nd August 1986, when section 17A was inserted in the Mines 
and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, reservation for exploitation by 
the Central and the State Public Sector undertakings were done by the State 
Governments under Rule 58 of the Mineral Concession Rules 1960. Thereafter, till the 
omission of rule 58 of Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 on the 13th April 1988, the State 
Governments were empowered to reserve mineral bearing areas for exploitation both 
by the Central and State Public Sector Undertakings. 
  
The Courts have held that all reservations made under rule 58 of the Mineral 
Concession Rules, 1960 till 13th April 1988 continue to be valid till these are rescinded. 
Therefore, the reference to erstwhile rule 58 of theMineral Concession Rules, 1960 in 
the proviso to rule 59 (1) (e) (ii) continue to be relevant.   
  
            Committee’s observations 
            The Committee noted the Ministry's reply. 
  
XVII    Point referred Rule 64 (A): - 
  
“The State Government may, without prejudice to the provisions contained in 
the Act or any other rule in these rules, charge simple interest at the rate of twenty 
four per cent   per annum on any rent, royalty or fee other than the fee payable under 
sub-rule (1) of rule   54 or other sum due to that Government under the Act or theses 
rules or under the terms and conditions of any prospecting license or mining lease from 
the sixtieth day of the expiry of the date fixed by that Government for payment of such 
royalty, rent, fee or other  sum and until payment of such royalty, rent, fee or other 
sum is made.” 
  
            The rate of interest to be charged for default in payment of rent, royalty or fee or 
other sum due to the Government is on the higher side.  Whether Government have any 
objection in reducing the rate of interest up to 12 or 15 per cent keeping in view the 
current economic scenario of reduced interest rates on capital? 
  
Ministry’s reply 

The rate of interest prescribed under the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 
purports to be penal interest. Mining dues are the most important source of non-tax 
revenue of the State Governments. The lessee is expected to pay the mining dues on 
schedule. Even the Prime Lending Rate (PLR) of Interest is 14 per cent. Any lowering 
of rate of interest could encourage the lessee to indulge in practices to the detriment of 
revenue interest of the State Governments, mineral conservation and development.  
             
Committee’s observations 
            The Committee noted the Ministry's reply.

3.         Thereafter on the 16th August, 2002, the Ministry furnished the following Action 
Taken Note on point no. 8 regarding the term ‘Dead Rent’ and point no. 11 regarding 
the term ‘Determination and Determine’: -  
            “Department of Mines in their earlier comments on Point No. 8 and Point No. 11 
have explained that the term dead rent, determination are precise terms in law 
and therefore, these have not been separately defined in Mines and Minerals 
(Development & Regulation) Act, 1957 or the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960. For 
instance, Osborn’s Concise Law Dictionary (Universal Law Publishing Co. Pvt. 
Ltd, 1993) defines “dead rent” as the minimum rent payable under a mining 
lease,’ “determination” as “to come to an end”.  These terms “dead rent” and 
“determination” are defined in Law in precise terms, and therefore, these terms 
were not separately defined in the Mines and Minerals (Development & 
Regulation) Act, 1957 or in the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960. Also, so far, no 
instances have come to the notice of the Government where the definition and 
application of these terms dead rent, determination or determine as used in the 

Mines and Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957 and the Mineral 
Concession Rules, 1960 have been challenged. 
                        The matter has been examined in consultation with the Ministry of Law 
and Justice, Department of Legal Affairs. 
                        The Ministry of Law in support of the contention of the Department that 
the natural meaning of the words under reference I normally adhered to in the 
absence of a definition in the statutes/rules and it has not so far had any 
implication or challenge in the Court of Law, have cited the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court judgment in the case of Ajay Pradhan Vs. State of M.P.  AIR 1988 SC 
1975.  The relevant extracts from the judgment are reproduced below: 
            “A rule must be interpreted by the written text.  If the precise word used are 
plain and unambiguous, the statute/rules and it has not so far had any legal 
implication or challenge in the Court is bound to construe them in their ordinary 
sense and give them full effect.  The plea of inconvenience and hardship is a 
dangerous one and is only admissible in construction where the meaning of the 
statute is obscure and there are alternative methods of construction. Where the 
language is explicit its consequences are for Parliament, and not for the Courts, 
to consider.” 
                                    In view of the legal opinion, therefore, the definition of ‘dead rent’ 
and ‘determination/determine’ in the mining statute is not required, as these 
terms are not intended to give any specific meaning other than their natural 
meaning to these words. 
                                    The above issues with the approval of competent authority.”

II 
The Cochin Port Employees (Classification, 
Control and Appeal) Regulations, 1964 
  
            The Committee examined the Cochin Port Trust Employees (Classification, 
Control and Appeal), Regulations, 1964 framed under the Major Port Trusts Act,

2.         The Committee discussed the subject matter with the representatives of the 
Cochin Port Trust and the Ministry of Shipping at Cochin on the 17th February 

1997.  The relevant extracts from the study note on the discussions were forwarded to 
the Ministry on the 18th November 1997 for their comments.  The Ministry of Shipping 
vides their communications dated the 28th August 1998 and the 2nd November 2000

Point No.1

            III 
Vishakapatnam Port Employees (GPF) Regulations, 1993 
  
      The Vishakapatnam Port Employees (GPF) Regulations, 1993 framed under the 
Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 were examined and a questionnaire on the subject was 
forwarded to the Ministry of Shipping on the 10th October, 2001 for their comments on 
the issues raised therein.  The points raised by the Committee and the Ministry’s 
comments thereon are at Annexure-I. 
2.                  The matter was taken up with the representatives of the Vishakapatnam Port 
Trust along with the Ministry of Shipping on the 9th November 2001 during the 
Committee’s study visit to Vishakapatnam.  During the course of discussions, the 
Ministry had agreed to the Committee’s suggestions on point nos. 2,3,5 and 9.  The 
Committee noted  the Ministry’s comments on the remaining points. Relevant extracts 
from the study note on the above discussion were forwarded to the Ministry on the 1st 
February 2002 for necessary action.  The Ministry vides their communications dated 
the 3rd April, 2002 and the 7th August, 2002 forwarded the Action Taken Note on the 
subject.  The Points referred, the Ministry’s comments, Committee’s further 
observations and the action taken by the Ministry on point Nos. 2,3,5 and 9 are as under 
:- 
  
1.    Point 2 – Regulation 2(5)(i) & (ii) 
Point referred: 
“In Regulation-2 (5)(i) in respect of male subscriber, it was mentioned that the 
subscriber has to intimate in writing to Accounts Officer, whereas in Regulation-
2(5)(ii) in respect of female subscriber, it was mentioned that the subscriber has 
to intimate in writing to the Head of the Department.  Whether the Government 
have any objection in prescribing a uniform procedure for both male and female 
employees?” 
  
Ministry’s observations 
      It is to submit that in the case of male subscriber, the nature of disqualifications has 
been mentioned as (1) his wife has been judiciously separated from him or (2) has 
ceased under the  
  

customary law of community to which she belongs to be entitled to maintenance, she 
shall henceforth be no longer a member of the subscriber’s family in matters to which 
these Regulations relate, unless the subscriber subsequently intimates in writing to the 
Accounts Officer that she shall continue to be so regarded.  Whereas in the case of 
female subscriber, no such disqualifications have been mentioned in the 
proviso.  However, in the case of female subscriber, it was mentioned that she has to 
give notice in writing to the Head of the Department expressing her desire to exclude 
her husband.  In this proviso, the disqualifications mentioned in the proviso, in respect 
of male subscriber has not been referred to and a power to cancel the said notice has 
also been given to the female subscriber.  However, to be on par with the Central 
Government Rules, steps will be taken to substitute the term ‘Head of Department’ with 
the term “Accounts Officer” in respect of female subscribers. 
  
Committee’s Observations  
      The Committee noted that the Ministry has agreed to have the words “Head of 
Department” substituted by the words “Accounts Officer” in respect of female 
employees for the sake of uniformity. 
  
Ministry’s comments (3.4.2002) 
      The Port Trust have proposed to amend the Regulations incorporating the words 
“Head of Department” substituting the words “Accounts Officer”.  However, the Port 
Trust are being asked to send consolidated proposal of the amendment taking into 
consideration all the points raised by the Committee on Subordinate Legislation. 
  
Port’s comments 
      The Port Trust agreed to amend the Regulations incorporating the words “Head of 
Department” substituting the words “Accounts Officer” 
  
Ministry’s comments (7.8.2002) 
      The amendment has been approved by the Government and the same is being 
published in the Gazette. 
  
2.    Point 3 – Regulation 2(5) 
Point referred 

“In respect of Regulation –2(5) note, the question is about the words “who lives 
with an employee” and whether this phrase include children who are away from 
employee for the purpose of studies but or otherwise depending on the 
employees?” 
  
Ministry’s comments (9.11.2001) 
      It is to submit that the note under Regulation – 2(5) is the replica of note under Rule 
2 (c)(ii) wherein the same phrase has been used.  In this connection, it is to submit that 
when the children of the employee are away for the purpose of studies, they cannot 
cease to be the children of the said employee, unless otherwise prohibited by law, 
because the children leave the association of the parents temporarily for a specified 
period.  So such Children cannot be excluded from the term child in Regulation-2 (5) 
note.  
  
Committee’s observations 
      The Committee noted that the Ministry appreciated the Committee’s viewpoint.  It 
desired the Ministry to examine whether position could be clarified in the Regulations. 
  
Ministry’s comments (3.4.2002) 
The Matter has already been taken up with the Vishakapatnam Port Trust vide this 
Ministry’s letter of even number dated the 26th November, 2001 for taking appropriate 
action.  They have been reminded of the same on the 28th February 2002. 
  
Port’s comments 
      The Port submitted to the Committee that the children of an employee couldn’t 
cease to be his children just because they are away for the purpose of studies.  Such 
children cannot be excluded from the term “Child” in Regulations 2(5) Note. 
  
Ministry’s comments (7.8.2002) 
The port is being asked to consider proposing a clarificatory note in the said Regulation 
in order to make the position clear. 
  
3.    Point 5 – Regulation 4(1) 
Point referred 

“With regard to Regulation-4(1), the existing Regulations indicate as if 
subscription of PF is only applicable to the employees, who have rendered 
continuous service of one year or more on the date of commencement of these 
Regulations.  The point for consideration is whether the employees joined after 
commencement of Regulations are covered under these Regulations or not?” 
  
Ministry’s comments (9.11.2001) 
      It is to submit that in Regulation 4(1), the commencement of recovery of PF 
subscription in respect of employees, who have rendered continuous service of one year 
or more, has been mentioned.  This Regulation also covers in respect of temporary 
employees who have not completed one year of service as on the date of commencement 
of these Regulations are also covered, by allowing recovery of subscription after 
completion of one year service, even though the date of completion of one year service 
has fallen after the commencement of these Regulations.  So, even in respect of 
employees who were appointed after the date of commencement of these Regulations 
will also be covered for recovery of PF subscriptions under these 
Regulations.  However, steps are being taken to clarify the position in the Regulation 
with respect to employees joining after issue of these Regulations. 
  
Committee’s observations  
      The Committee was satisfied that the Vishakapatnam Port Trust agreed to clarify 
the position in respect of employees joining the Port Trust after the issue of the 
Regulations in the Regulation itself. 
 
      Ministry’s comments (3.4.2002) 
      The Port Trust has already been asked to take action for amending the regulations 
as per suggestions of the Committee. 
  
Port’s comments 
      The Port has clarified that even in respect of employees, who were appointed after 
the commencement of these regulations, will also be required to subscribe to the 
Fund.  Accordingly, the Port is actively considering the question of amendment to the 
clause. 
  
Ministry’s comments (7.8.2002) 

      The Port Trust is being asked to send the necessary amendment proposal. 
  
4.    Point 9 – Regulation 14(1) (b) (ii) 
Point referred: 
      “With regard to Regulation – 14(1)(b)(ii), the point for consideration is what is the 
justification for prescribing the condition of not less than 3 years in this Regulation for 
granting advance for GPF, when there are technical courses which are expensive and 
with duration of less than 3 years?” 
  
Ministry’s comments (9.11.2001) 
      It is to submit that Rule 12 (1)(b)(ii) of the GPF (Central Services) Rules, 1960, the 
period was mentioned as 3 years and as such the same provision was incorporated in 
Regulation 14(1)(b) (ii) also of Vishakapatnam Port Trust Employees 
(GPF   Regulations), 1993.  Since the Port Regulations are mainly based on Central 
Government Rules, if the period of 3 years is amended in Rule 12(1)(b)(ii) of the GPF 
Rules of the Central Government similar amendment will also be made in Regulation – 
14 (1) (b)(ii) of the GPF Regulations. 
Committee’s observations  
      The Committee observed that there was no bar on the Port Trust to wait for the 
amendment in the GPF rules pertaining to Central Government.  They can amend their 
own regulation for the benefit of their employees.  The Committee informed that the 
representative of the Mormugao and the Madras Port Trust had already agreed to this 
suggestion of the Committee.  The Committee desired that the Ministry of Shipping 
should re-examine this point. 
  
Ministry’s comments (3.4.2002) 
      The Port Trust has already been asked to amend the regulation. 
  
Port’s comments (7.8.2002) 
The Port has framed their regulations on par with the CCS (GPF) Rules and since Port 
regulations are mainly based on the CCS Rules, if the period of 3 years is amended in 
Rule 12(1)(b)(ii) of the CCS (GPF) Rules, similar amendment would also be made in the 
Regulations. 
  
Ministry’s comments (7.8.2002) 

      The Ministry also feels that it is not advisable to make any deviation in the Port 
Trust GPF Regulations from the CCS Rule. 
  
3.      The Committee was not satisfied with the Ministry’s stand on Regulation 14(1)(b)(ii) 
and asked the Ministry on the 4th February, 2003 to review their stand in the light of 
the fact that similar amendment had already been accepted by them in the parallel 
regulation of the Madras Port Trust and the Mormugao Port Trust as contained in 
its 125th Report presented on the 22nd December, 1999. 
  
4.      The Ministry vide their communications dated the 17th January, 20th February & 
28th July, 2003 forwarded notifications G.S.R. 614 dated the 2nd September, 2002,

2003 amending the Vishakapatnam Port Trust Employees (GPF) Regulations, 1993 
as suggested by the Committee.  
  
5.   The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Ministry have notified the

      a)    Regulation 2(5)(ii) by substituting the words “Head of the Department” by the

spouse from family.  
      b)    Regulation 2(5) by amending the definition of the word “child” so as to include

purpose of studies but were otherwise dependent upon the employee. 
      c)    Regulation 4(1) by specifying the position in the regulation itself with regard to

      d)    Regulation 14(1)(b)(ii) by amending the provision so as to include Medical,
